The section is titled 'GRADIENT DESCENT AND COMPUTATIONAL GRAPHS'.
Gradient descent involves taking the gradient with respect to weights and moving in that direction.
Formally, for an error function $E$, targets $y$, and model $f$ with parameters $\theta$, $E(\theta) = \sum_{(x,y)\in D} E(f(x, \theta), y)$.
$\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \eta \nabla E(\theta_{t-1}) = \theta_{t-1} - \eta \sum_{(x,y)\in D} \nabla E(f(x, \theta_{t-1}), y)$.
It is necessary to sum over the entire dataset for every step of gradient descent.
Stochastic gradient descent updates after every training sample: $\theta_t = \theta_{t-1} - \eta \nabla E(f(x_t, \theta_{t-1}), y_t)$.
In practice, people usually use mini-batches.
Mini-batches are easy to parallelize.
Mini-batches smooth out excessive stochasticity.
So far, the only parameter is the learning rate $\eta$.
There are lots of problems with the learning rate $\eta$.
The lecture will address the problems with $\eta$ later.
For now, the lecture concentrates on the computation of derivatives.
A function can be represented as a composition of simple functions.
'Simple' functions are functions for which we can take derivatives.
An example function is $f(x, y) = x^2 + xy + (x + y)^2$.
Using the representation as a composition of simple functions, we can take the gradient with the chain rule: $(f \circ g)'(x) = (f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) g'(x)$.
An increment $\delta x$ results in $\delta f = f'(g(x)) \delta g = f'(g(x)) g'(x) \delta x$.
We only need to be able to take gradients, i.e., derivatives with respect to vectors.
The gradient of $f$ with respect to $x$ is $\nabla_x f = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}$.

The gradient of the composition $f \circ g$ is $\nabla_x (f \circ g) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f \circ g}{\partial x_1} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f \circ g}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial f}{\partial g} \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_1} \\ \vdots \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial g} \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\partial f}{\partial g} \nabla_x g$.
If $f$ depends on $x$ via multiple functions $f = f(g_1(x), g_2(x), \ldots, g_k(x))$, then the increment $\delta x$ appears in the chain rule multiple times.
In that case, $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\partial f}{\partial g_i} \frac{\partial g_i}{\partial x}$.
The gradient with respect to $x$ is $\nabla_x f = \sum_{i=1}^k \frac{\partial f}{\partial g_i} \nabla_x g_i$.

This results in matrix multiplication for the Jacobian: $
abla_x f = 
abla_x \mathbf{g} 
abla_{\mathbf{g}} f$.

The Jacobian matrix $\nabla_x \mathbf{g}$ is $\begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial g_1}{\partial x_1} & \ldots & \frac{\partial g_k}{\partial x_1} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\ \frac{\partial g_1}{\partial x_n} & \ldots & \frac{\partial g_k}{\partial x_n} \end{pmatrix}$.
Forward propagation computes $\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ using the chain rule.
Backpropagation computes gradients by starting from the end node and moving backward.
The gradient with respect to a node $g$ is given by $\frac{\partial f}{\partial g} = \sum_{g' \in \text{Children}(g)} \frac{\partial f}{\partial g'} \frac{\partial g'}{\partial g}$.
Backpropagation is much better than forward propagation because it computes all derivatives in a single pass through the graph.
With backpropagation, we can now compute the gradients of any complicated composition of simple functions.
Computing gradients of any composition of simple functions is all we need to apply gradient descent.
Libraries such as PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Theano are actually automatic differentiation libraries.
The main function of PyTorch, TensorFlow, and Theano is automatic differentiation.
Many 'classical' models can be implemented in TensorFlow and trained by gradient descent.
Live neurons cannot compute both the value and the derivative because they would need two different outputs.
The next section covers activation functions.
There are many different nonlinearities.
The lecture provides a brief survey of activation functions.
The logistic sigmoid is defined as $\sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}}$.
The hyperbolic tangent is defined as $\tanh(x) = \frac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}}$.
The hyperbolic tangent is very similar to the logistic sigmoid.
For the hyperbolic tangent, zero is not a saturation point.
The Heaviside step function is defined as $\text{step}(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ 1, & \text{if } x > 0 \end{cases}$.
The Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) is defined as $\text{ReLU}(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ x, & \text{if } x \ge 0 \end{cases}$.
There is a mathematical motivation for ReLU.

The mathematical motivation for ReLU involves the sum $\sigma(x + \frac{1}{2}) + \sigma(x - \frac{1}{2}) + \sigma(x - \frac{3}{2}) + \sigma(x - \frac{5}{2}) + \ldots$ where $\sigma$ is the logistic sigmoid.
There is a biological motivation for ReLU.

The biological motivation for ReLU is a function $f(I)$ defined as $f(I) = \begin{cases} \left( \tau \log \frac{E + R I - V_{\text{reset}}}{E + R I - V_{th}} \right)^{-1}, & \text{if } E + R I > V_{th} \\ 0, & \text{if } E + R I \le V_{th} \end{cases}$.
There are several ReLU variations.
Softplus is defined as $\text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x)$.
Leaky ReLU (LReLU) is defined as $\text{LReLU}(x) = \begin{cases} a x, & \text{if } x < 0 \\ x, & \text{if } x > 0 \end{cases}$.
Exponential Linear Unit (ELU) is defined as $\text{ELU}(x) = \begin{cases} \alpha (e^x - 1), & x < 0 \\ x, & x \ge 0 \end{cases}$.
The slide includes a plot comparing ReLU, Softplus, Leaky ReLU with different parameters, and ELU with different $\alpha$ values.
The activation functions mentioned so far are only a beginning.
Ramachandran et al. (2017) performed an automated search over function space.
Ramachandran et al. (2017) discovered the Swish activation function.
Swish is defined as $\text{Swish}(x) = x \sigma(\beta x) = \frac{x}{1 + e^{-\beta x}}$.
Misra (2019) proposed Mish activation function.
Mish is defined as $\text{Mish}(x) = x \tanh(\text{softplus}(x)) = x \tanh(\ln(1 + e^x))$.
A plot in the slide compares ReLU, Swish with different $\beta$, and Mish.
The most interesting development in activation functions happened in 2020.
Ma et al. (2020) proposed a smooth generalization of the maximum, $S_\beta(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n x_i e^{\beta x_i}}{\sum_{i=1}^n e^{\beta x_i}}$.

Substituting two functions of $x$ into $S_\beta$, to approximate $\max(g(x), h(x))$, yields $S_\beta(g(x), h(x)) = g(x) \frac{e^{\beta g(x)}}{e^{\beta g(x)} + e^{\beta h(x)}} + h(x) \frac{e^{\beta h(x)}}{e^{\beta g(x)} + e^{\beta h(x)}}$.
The expression $S_\beta(g(x), h(x))$ simplifies to $(g(x) - h(x)) \sigma(\beta (g(x) - h(x))) + h(x)$.
Ma et al. (2020) named the construction ActivateOrNot (ACON).
The ACON construction generalizes previous activation functions.
For $g(x) = x$ and $h(x) = 0$, the hard maximum is $\text{ReLU}(x) = \max(x, 0)$, and the soft maximum becomes $f_{ACON-A}(x) = S_\beta(x, 0) = x \sigma(\beta x)$, which is exactly Swish.
For $g(x) = x$ and $h(x) = a x$ with $a < 1$, the hard maximum is LReLU, and the soft maximum is $f_{ACON-B} = S_\beta(x, a x) = (1 - a) x \sigma(\beta (1 - a) x) + a x$.
The ACON construction can be further generalized to $f_{ACON-C} = S_\beta(a_1 x, a_2 x) = (a_1 - a_2) x \sigma(\beta (a_1 - a_2) x) + a_2 x$.
In ACON-C, $a_1$ and $a_2$ can be learnable parameters.
Intuitively, $a_1$ and $a_2$ represent the limits of the derivative on both sides: $\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{d f_{ACON-C}}{dx} = a_1$, $\lim_{x \to -\infty} \frac{d f_{ACON-C}}{dx} = a_2$.

The slide shows a plot of ACON-C for various parameter values: $(a_1=1, a_2=0, \beta=1)$, $(a_1=1.2, a_2=-0.1, \beta=1)$, $(a_1=1, a_2=-0.8, \beta=1)$, $(a_1=1, a_2=-0.8, \beta=0.1)$, $(a_1=1, a_2=-0.8, \beta=0.01)$.
Ma et al. (2020) show that by tuning the parameters one can win a lot even in standard tasks.
The author has not seen much of ACON-C in actual practice.
This just goes to show that deep learning has a lot of not-very-hidden depths even in the simplest things.
The next section covers variations of gradient descent.
'Vanilla' gradient descent update is $x_k = x_{k-1} - \alpha \nabla f(x_k)$.
Much depends on the learning rate $\alpha$ in gradient descent.
One idea is to let the learning rate $\alpha$ decrease with time.
Linear decay of learning rate: $\alpha = \alpha_0 (1 - \frac{t}{T})$.
Exponential decay of learning rate: $\alpha = \alpha_0 e^{-t/T}$.
There are many results regarding step size selection, including the Wolfe conditions.
In the minimization problem $\min_x f(x)$, at step $k$, given a descent direction $p_k$ (e.g., $p_k = \nabla_x f(x_k)$), we need to solve $\min_{\alpha} f(x_k + \alpha p_k)$.
Define $\phi_k(\alpha) = f(x_k + \alpha p_k)$, then $\phi_k'(\alpha) = \nabla f(x_k + \alpha p_k)^\top p_k$.
If $p_k$ is a descent direction, then $\phi_k'(0) < 0$.
The Armijo rule requires the step size $\alpha$ to satisfy $\phi_k(\alpha) \le \phi_k(0) + c_1 \alpha \phi_k'(0)$ for some $c_1 \in (0, \frac{1}{2})$.
The Wolfe conditions include the stronger Wolfe's rule: Armijo rule plus $|\phi_k'(\alpha)| \le c_2 |\phi_k'(0)|$.
Wolfe's rule aims to ensure a decrease in the projection of the gradient.

The optimization process stops when $\|
abla_x f(x_k)\|_2 \le \epsilon$ or $\|
abla_x f(x_k)\|_2 \le \epsilon \|
abla_x f(x_0)\|_2$.
An example function to consider scale effects is $f(x, y) = \frac{1}{2} x^2 + \frac{\rho}{2} y^2$ to be minimized.
When variables have different scales (elongated 'valleys'), gradient descent takes many superfluous iterations and is very slow.
It would be much better to use an adaptive method.
Newton's method scales the gradient with the inverse Hessian.
In Newton's method, $g_k = \nabla_x f(x_k)$, $H_k = \nabla^2_x f(x_k)$, and the update is $x_{k+1} = x_k - \alpha_k H_k^{-1} g_k$.
The Armijo rule can be applied to Newton's method: choose $\alpha_k$ such that $f(x_{k+1}) \le f(x_k) - c_1 \alpha_k g_k^\top H_k^{-1} g_k$ with $c_1 \approx 10^{-4}$.
Newton's method would be very nice, but one cannot simply compute the Hessian $H_k$.
There are approximations to Newton's method.
Conjugate gradients and quasi-Newton methods are among the approximations.
L-BFGS (limited memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno) is one such approximation method.
L-BFGS constructs an approximation to the inverse Hessian $H^{-1}$.
L-BFGS saves updates of the arguments and then expresses $H^{-1}$ through them.
An important open question is whether L-BFGS or similar methods can work for deep learning.
So far, L-BFGS does not work for deep learning.
The main reason L-BFGS does not work is that it requires computing the gradient, and in deep learning we are not computing the full gradient.
Stochastic gradient descent uses the update $x_t = x_{t-1} - \alpha \nabla f(x_t, x_{t-1}, y_t)$.
Mini-batches are also used in stochastic gradient descent.
Stochastic gradient descent can be understood formally via stochastic optimization problems.
A stochastic optimization problem is of the form $F(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q(y)} f(x, y) \to \min_x$.
Empirical risk minimization is a special case: $F(x) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x) = \mathbb{E}_{i \sim U(1,\ldots,N)} f_i(x) \to \min_x$.
Another example is variational lower bound (ELBO) minimization, which will be discussed later.
Empirical estimates of a random function from a sample are given by $\hat{F}(x) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m f(x, y_i)$ and $\hat{g}(x) = \frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^m \nabla_x f(x, y_i)$.
These estimates are unbiased, converge (albeit slowly), and are easy to compute.
Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is motivated as a Monte-Carlo approach.
SGD has problems.
One problem with SGD is that it never goes in the exact right direction.
Another problem is that even at the exact optimum of $F(x)$, the step is nonzero, so SGD cannot converge with a constant step size.
We know neither 𝐹(x) nor ∇𝐹(x), so we cannot use Armijo and Wolfe’s rules.
We can try to analyze an SGD iteration for 𝐹(x) = 𝔼_{q(y)} 𝑓(x, y) to minimize x.
The SGD iteration is: x_{k+1} = x_k - α_k ĝ_k, where ĝ_k is a stochastic gradient estimate.
The expected value of the stochastic gradient estimate ĝ_k equals the true gradient g_k = ∇𝐹(x_k).

The squared distance to the optimum after one SGD update is ‖x_{k+1} - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 = ‖x_k - α_k ĝ_k - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 = ‖x_k - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 - 2α_k ĝ_k^{\top}(x_k - x_{\text{opt}}) + α_k^2 ‖ĝ_k‖^2.
Taking expectation with respect to q(y) at time k gives: 𝔼‖x_{k+1} - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 = ‖x_k - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 - 2α_k g_k^{\top}(x_k - x_{\text{opt}}) + α_k^2 𝔼‖ĝ_k‖^2, where g_k = ∇𝐹(x_k).
Assuming 𝐹 is convex, we have 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}}) ≥ 𝐹(x_k) + g_k^{\top}(x_k - x_{\text{opt}}).
From the two previous equations we derive: α_k(𝐹(x_k) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}})) ≤ \frac{1}{2} ‖x_k - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 + \frac{1}{2} α_k^2 𝔼‖ĝ_k‖^2 - \frac{1}{2} 𝔼‖x_{k+1} - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2.

Summing these inequalities from i = 0 to k and taking expectation yields: ∑_{i=0}^k α_i(𝔼𝐹(x_i) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}})) ≤ \frac{1}{2} ‖x_0 - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 + \frac{1}{2} ∑_{i=0}^k α_i^2 𝔼‖ĝ_i‖^2 - \frac{1}{2} 𝔼‖x_{k+1} - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 ≤ \frac{1}{2} ‖x_0 - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 + \frac{1}{2} ∑_{i=0}^k α_i^2 𝔼‖ĝ_i‖^2.
Using convexity, we obtain 𝔼𝐹(∑_i α_i x_i / ∑_i α_i) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}}) ≤ \frac{\frac{1}{2} ‖x_0 - x_{\text{opt}}‖^2 + \frac{1}{2} ∑_{i=0}^k α_i^2 𝔼‖ĝ_i‖^2}{∑_i α_i}.
The estimate is on the value at a linear combination of points; in practice it is equivalent or better to take the last point.

If the initial distance is bounded by R (‖x_0 - x_{\text{opt}}‖ ≤ R) and the expected squared norm of the stochastic gradient is bounded by G^2 (𝔼‖ĝ_k‖^2 ≤ G^2), then 𝔼𝐹(X_k) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}}) ≤ (R^2 + G^2 ∑_{i=0}^k α_i^2) / (2 ∑_{i=0}^k α_i), where X_k = ∑_i α_i x_i / ∑_i α_i.
The main bound for SGD is 𝔼𝐹(X_k) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}}) ≤ (R^2 + G^2 ∑_{i=0}^k α_i^2) / (2 ∑_{i=0}^k α_i).
R is an estimate of the initial distance to the optimum, and G is an estimate of something like the variance (or second moment) of the stochastic gradient.
For constant step size α_i = h, 𝔼𝐹(X_k) - 𝐹(x_{\text{opt}}) ≤ R^2/(2h(k+1)) + G^2 h/2, which tends to G^2 h/2 as k → ∞.
SGD converges to an "uncertainty region" of radius (1/2) G^2 h, which is proportional to the step size h.
The faster the learning (larger step size), the faster SGD reaches the uncertainty region, but the larger that region becomes; therefore, the learning rate should be decreased over time.
For convex functions, full gradient descent has convergence rate O(1/k) (in terms of residue), while SGD has rate O(1/√k).

Far from the uncertainty region, SGD with constant learning rate still achieves O(1/k) convergence in residue; it slows down only near the optimum, and the practical goal is to reach the uncertainty region.
The convergence depends on G (the bound on the second moment of the stochastic gradient), which is especially important for neurobayesian approaches.
There is a need for improvements to SGD, particularly regarding the learning rate.
It is better not to decrease the learning rate too quickly.
However, standard SGD does not directly account for the objective function 𝐹 itself in its adaptation.
SGD with momentum keeps part of the previous velocity, analogous to inertia in physics.
The momentum update rule is: u_t = γ u_{t-1} + η ∇_{\text{x}} 𝐹(\text{x}), and \text{x} ← \text{x} - u_t.
The term γ u_{t-1} is preserved from the previous step.
We already know that we will move to the intermediate point γ u_{t-1}.
The suggestion is to compute the gradient at that intermediate point.
Nesterov's momentum (Nesterov accelerated gradient) uses the update rule: u_t = γ u_{t-1} + η ∇_{\text{x}} 𝐹(\text{x} - γ u_{t-1}).
Previously, gradient descent used the same learning rate for all parameter directions.
The idea of adaptive gradient descent is to move faster along parameter axes that change slowly and slower along those that change rapidly.
Adagrad takes into account the history of gradient updates.

The Adagrad update for parameter i is: w_{t+1,i} = w_{t,i} - (η / √(G_{t,ii} + ϵ)) · g_{t,i}, where G_t is a diagonal matrix with G_{t,ii} = G_{t-1,ii} + g_{t,i}^2, accumulating the sum of squared gradients over the entire history.
Thus, the effective learning rate keeps decreasing over time, but at different rates for different parameters.
A problem with Adagrad is that G keeps increasing, so the learning rate monotonically decreases and never recovers.
Adadelta (Zeiler, 2012) is a modification of Adagrad with two changes.
First, Adadelta uses an exponential moving average of squared gradients: G_{t,ii} = ρ G_{t-1,ii} + (1 - ρ) g_{t,i}^2.
Then the update is similar: u_t = - (η / √(G_{t-1} + ϵ)) g_{t-1}.
Second, Adadelta addresses the issue of unit compatibility between parameter updates and gradients.

In regular gradient descent or momentum, the units of parameter updates are the units of the gradient, leading to a mismatch in scales (e.g., weights in seconds, gradient in meters per second, subtracting meters per second from seconds).
In Adagrad, the parameter updates are dimensionless because they come from ratios of gradients, which is also problematic.
In second-order optimization, the parameter update Δw is proportional to the inverse Hessian times the gradient, and naturally has the same dimension as w.
To fix the unit issue in Adadelta, an exponential moving average of squared parameter updates is introduced.

The exponential moving average of squared parameter updates is computed as 𝔼[Δw^2]_t = ρ 𝔼[Δw^2]_{t-1} + (1 - ρ) Δw^2, and the update becomes u_t = - (√(𝔼[Δw^2]_{t-1} + ϵ) / √(G_{t-1} + ϵ)) · g_{t-1}.
RMSprop is a variant often mentioned, with no formal publication, originating from Hinton's lectures.
RMSprop is essentially Adadelta without the unit correction; its update is u_t = - (η / √(G_{t-1} + ϵ)) · g_{t-1}.
Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2014) is another adaptive optimization algorithm.
Adam uses smoothed (exponential moving average) versions of the gradient (first moment) and squared gradient (second moment).
The moment estimates are: m_t = β_1 m_{t-1} + (1 - β_1) g_t, v_t = β_2 v_{t-1} + (1 - β_2) g_t^2.
The parameter update is: u_t = η / (√v_t + ϵ) m_t.
The recommended Adam hyperparameters are β_1 = 0.9, β_2 = 0.999, ϵ = 10^{-8}.
Adam requires little hyperparameter tuning and is widely used in practice.
Nadam (Dozat, 2016) is a combination of Adam and Nesterov momentum.
Vanilla SGD update is w_{k+1} = w_k - α_k ṻ f(w_k), where ṻ f(w_k) is the stochastic gradient computed on data point x_{i_k}.
SGD with momentum update is w_{k+1} = w_k - α_k ṻ f(w_k + γ_k (w_k - w_{k-1})) + β_k (w_k - w_{k-1}).

Adaptive SGD generalizes to w_{k+1} = w_k - α_k H_k^{-1} ṻ f(w_k + γ_k (w_k - w_{k-1})) + β_k H_k^{-1} H_{k-1} (w_k - w_{k-1}), where H_k = \text{diag}([\sum_{i=1}^k η_i g_i ∘ g_i]^{1/2}), with g_k = ṻ f(w_k + γ_k (w_k - w_{k-1})).
Adaptive methods attempt to adapt to the data space geometry, whereas basic SGD uses the standard Euclidean (L2) geometry with H_k = I.
When Adam was introduced, it generated significant excitement.
When multiple global minima exist, different optimization algorithms can converge to different solutions from the same initial point.
Adaptive methods can lead to overfitting, finding solutions that generalize poorly.
This overfitting behavior of adaptive methods is not just a theoretical worst-case scenario; it occurs in practice.
Adam still performs very well in the early stages of training.
Some researchers suggest switching from Adam to SGD at an appropriate moment (Keskar and Socher, Dec 2017).
Weight decay is commonly assumed to be equivalent to L2 regularization.
However, this equivalence does not hold exactly for adaptive methods.
The original weight decay update (Hanson and Pratt, 1988) is: x_{t+1} = (1 - w) x_t - η ∇f_t(x_t), with weight decay rate w and learning rate η.
This weight decay is equivalent to adding an L2 regularization term (w/2)‖x_t‖^2 to the objective function.
Equivalently, the gradient of the regularized objective is ∇f_t(x) + w x_t.
With momentum, weight decay does not behave as intended because the decay term becomes scaled by the learning rate, leading to a coupling between the learning rate and weight decay hyperparameters.
One solution is to apply weight decay directly to the parameter update, decoupling it from the adaptive learning rate scaling.
In standard Adam, parameters with large gradients experience less weight decay, which can be detrimental.
AdamW restores the original weight decay behavior by decoupling it from the adaptive gradient scaling.
AdamW decouples the weight decay hyperparameter from the learning rate, leading to better disentanglement.
AdamW achieves better generalization compared to standard Adam.
Two more interesting ideas are super-convergence and AMSGrad.
Super-convergence (Smith and Topin, 2017) proposes cyclical learning rate schedules.
Super-convergence combines ideas from curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) and classical simulated annealing.
However, super-convergence does not consistently reproduce results across settings.
AMSGrad (Reddi et al., 2018) won the ICLR 2018 best paper award.
The exponential moving average in Adam and RMSprop can hurt convergence.
The original proof of Adam's convergence was incorrect.
AMSGrad keeps the maximum of past squared gradients (instead of exponential moving average), which theoretically improves convergence.
However, the practical benefits of AMSGrad over Adam are not clearly confirmed.
